solution:
**(B)** capillary water

Capillary water is held in the pores between neighbouring soil particles by capillarity, and it is the only form of soil water available to roots for absorption. Gravitational water percolates deep below the root zone, hygroscopic water is held too tightly by fine soil particles, and combined water is locked in hydrated oxides of silicon and aluminium, so none of these can be absorbed.

**(D)** transpiration pull theory

The cohesion-tension theory, or transpiration pull theory, of Dixon and Jolly (1894) is the presently widely accepted explanation for the ascent of sap. Capillarity lifts water only a few centimetres, and root pressure cannot work in plants taller than about 20 metres or in actively transpiring plants. Diffusion is far too slow to move water up a stem.

**(C)** D.P.D.

Water moves from a cell with lower DPD (suction pressure) to an adjacent cell with higher DPD, which is why a gradient of DPD carries water from the root hair across the cortex. Turgor pressure and wall pressure are pressures within one cell, and incipient plasmolysis is a state of a cell, not a force that moves water between cells.

**(A)** closes almost completely

By the starch-sugar interconversion theory, sugar in the guard cells raises their osmotic concentration so they take in water, become turgid and open the stoma. When sugar is converted back to starch (at night), the osmotic concentration falls, water leaves by exosmosis, the guard cells become flaccid and the stoma closes almost completely.

**(D)** cohesion

Surface tension arises because water molecules at the surface are pulled inward by the attraction of like molecules, that is cohesion, which in water comes from hydrogen bonding. Diffusion and osmosis are movements of molecules, not forces at a surface, and gravity acts against the rise of water rather than producing surface tension.

[Note: the chapter links surface tension and cohesion to capillarity but does not state this cause directly; standard biology gives cohesion between water molecules as the cause of surface tension.]

**(B)** Hypotonic

A hypotonic solution is a weak solution with a low osmotic concentration, so it has fewer solutes than the solution it is compared with (the stem as printed means the other solution, such as the cell sap). A hypertonic solution has more solutes, an isotonic one has the same concentration, and anisotonic only means "not equal" without saying which side is lower.

**(B)** imbibition

Wood is made of cellulose and other hydrophilic colloids, which adsorb moisture from the humid air in the rainy season and swell up. This swelling of hydrophilic colloids by adsorption of water is imbibition. Osmosis and plasmolysis need a semipermeable membrane and living cells, which dry wood does not have.

**(C)** root hair

In the zone of absorption, epiblema cells form unicellular root hairs, and water enters through them by imbibition, diffusion and osmosis in sequence. The root cap only protects the tip, and the older surfaces of the primary and lateral roots lack root hairs and absorb little water.

**(A)** increase

Low atmospheric pressure makes water evaporate more readily from the leaf and lets water vapour diffuse away faster, so the rate of transpiration rises. This is why plants at high altitudes, where air pressure is low, tend to transpire more and often show xerophytic features.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives an increase in transpiration at low atmospheric pressure.]

**(C)** solution

Osmosis, and the osmotic pressure it produces, is a colligative property of a solution: it depends on the concentration of solute particles dissolved in the solvent. It is the solvent that moves, but the cause is the difference in concentration between two solutions across the membrane, and the membrane only allows the process to happen.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology treats osmotic pressure as a colligative property of a solution.]
